findings.where: First screen, desktop and phone: the row of five outlined pills under Mark's lead paragraph (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation)
findings.fault: The pills do nothing when clicked (parts.txt p10–p14: static), but they look clickable. Each has its own rounded outline and the semibold sans that the nav and the action use, so they read as topic filters or tag links into Articles and Blog. They also sit just above the one real action and share its white-on-blue treatment, so a visitor sees two kinds of button on a screen meant to have one action.
findings.who_objects: Staff at a development bank who want Mark's writing on one subject, such as PPP Law or risk allocation, would click a pill to get there. Nothing happens, and on a first visit a dead control looks like a broken site. That weakens the trust a solo advisor's homepage depends on.

findings.where: Article specimen, desktop and phone: the lecture link 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge' and the bullets of the three-item list above it
findings.fault: This link is underlined in orange-red, but 'Play again', the other link on the white page, is house blue, and the palette says links on white are house blue. Two different looks mean 'link' on one surface. The list bullets also use the same orange-red, so the link's own colour is used for decoration a few lines above it.
findings.who_objects: A reader of Mark's articles has to learn two link colours. Since the bullets are coloured like the link, the reader may take the list items as links, or stop trusting colour as the cue. Angélique, adding articles, has no single rule for what a link looks like.
